name: Morpeth Court
text: Your train passes near the old courthouse, on the train's {side}, the castle-like gatehouse of a prison that John Dobson designed and finished in 1828. When the magistrates left in 1980 it became a nightclub, then a ladies-only health club, and it is now flats.

name: Bomarsund, Northumberland
text: Your train passes Bomarsund, on the train's {side}, a village that grew round a coal pit opened in 1854 and took its name from a fortress in the Åland Islands, now part of Finland, fought over in the Crimean War that year. Its cricket team won the National Village Championship in 1974, at Edgbaston after the final at Lord's was rained off.

name: Bedlington Academy
text: Your train passes close to a secondary school, on the train's {side}, founded in 1926 beside the old station. Bobby Charlton was a pupil there when it was a grammar school.

name: Blyth Bebside railway station
text: Blyth Bebside station, at one end of this stretch, opened in October 2025. It replaced a station of 1850, first called Cowpen Lane, which closed in 1964.

name: New Hartley Ponds
text: Your train passes New Hartley Ponds, on the train's {side}, six seasonal ponds that are a Site of Special Scientific Interest. Frogs, toads and newts breed there, with up to 500 great crested newts and 1,000 smooth newts.

name: Seghill railway station
text: Your train passes the site of Seghill station, opened in 1841 by the Blyth, Seghill and Percy Main Railway. The goods it handled were mostly bricks, clay and ganister, and it closed for good in 1965.

name: Ashington Colliery Junction railway station
text: Your train passes the site of Ashington Colliery Junction station, on the train's {side}, open from 1871 to 1878. No road came near it, so it was probably used by railway staff or miners, and in 1877 its only train called at 3.30pm on Saturdays.

name: Chevington railway station
text: Your train passes the site of Chevington station, on the train's {side}, open from 1847 until 1958. A mile north of it, a branch left for the port of Amble from 1849, though passenger trains didn't run on it for another 30 years.

name: Warkworth railway station
text: Your train passes the site of Warkworth station, opened in 1847 and designed by Benjamin Green. By 1951 it sold only 1,023 tickets a year, about three a day; it closed to passengers in 1958, and the station house still stands.

name: Fallodon
text: Your train passes near Fallodon, on the train's {side}, the Grey family's estate, from which Sir Edward Grey took his title, Viscount Grey of Fallodon. A small station near the hall, opened in 1847 for the family's own use, lasted until 1934.

name: Royal Border Bridge
text: Your train crosses the Tweed on the Royal Border Bridge, Robert Stephenson's viaduct of 28 arches, 37 metres above the river, opened by Queen Victoria in 1850. Despite its name, it doesn't cross the border: Scotland is about three miles further north.

name: Berwick Castle
text: Your train passes the ruins of Berwick Castle, on the train's {side}, built for David I of Scotland in the 1120s. Its great hall, where Edward I's choice of John Balliol as King of Scotland was announced in 1292, was pulled down in 1847 to make way for the station.

name: Hepscott
text: Your train passes near Hepscott, on the train's {side}, a village whose Anglo-Saxon name comes from 'Shepherd's Cote'. Its oldest building, Hepscott Hall, is a three-storey medieval pele tower that once had a deer park.

name: St Mary's Church, Gateshead
text: Your train passes near St Mary's Church, on the train's {side}, which was the only church in Gateshead until the 1820s. Damaged by fire in 1979 and restored, it has reopened as the town's first heritage centre.

name: Trinity Square, Gateshead
text: Your train passes near Trinity Square, on the train's {side}, a shopping centre opened in 2013 where the Brutalist multi-storey car park from the 1971 film 'Get Carter' stood. Designed in 1962 and opened in 1967, the car park was pulled down in 2010.
